opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it looks like chance from the outside, but from the inside it feels more like a series of small, ordinary decisions that kept compounding.

With Kaiming, for example, I was a PhD student and came in as an intern. I didn't have some grand plan. I was just very curious and wanted to work on problems I thought were fundamental. What I learned was that the collaboration wasn't really about the internship. It was about whether you could share a certain taste in research. Kaiming has a very particular style: very simple ideas, very careful experiments, and a lot of patience in removing everything unnecessary. If you resonate with that, the conversation naturally keeps going. It doesn't end when the internship ends.

With Fei-Fei it was similar in a way, though at a different stage of my career. By then I was thinking a lot about what's missing in today's models, about vision not just as recognition but as understanding space and the physical world. She had been thinking about related questions from her own direction for a long time. When two people independently arrive at a similar question, working together feels less like an arrangement and more like recognizing each other.

So I'd say the encounters may be random, but whether they turn into collaborations isn't. It depends on whether you've already been thinking seriously about something, so that when you meet the right person, you actually have something to talk about. Luck gives you the meeting. Your own questions decide what happens after.

I also think it's important to be open and a bit naive. Many students hesitate to reach out or to show half-baked ideas. But the people I've learned the most from were very generous with half-baked ideas themselves. Research is a social process. It's very human. A lot of good work comes from long conversations, not from one person sitting alone with a brilliant insight.

r001.rationale: The response says collaborations grew from sharing a research taste and independently arriving at similar questions, rather than from chance alone.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think any of them were really chance encounters, to be honest. They look like luck in hindsight, but each one grew out of a shared problem we were both already circling.

With Kaiming, the connection came through Piotr Dollár and Ross Girshick at FAIR. Kaiming had done ResNet, Ross had done Fast R-CNN, and I showed up with this question about why wider or deeper wasn't the only axis you could scale. That became ResNeXt. What made it a real collaboration rather than a one-off was that we kept running into the same confusion. We'd each have a half-formed intuition, and talking it through at the whiteboard turned it into an experiment by the afternoon. Kaiming is unusually good at stripping a problem down to the one thing that matters, and I learned a lot just from watching him say "no" to ideas, including mine.

Fei-Fei was different. I'd known her work since graduate school, obviously, because ImageNet was the water we were all swimming in. But the actual collaboration only started when I moved to NYU and we found ourselves asking the same uncomfortable question from opposite ends: what is a visual representation actually for, once you have language models that seem to get vision "for free"? She came at it from cognition and spatial intelligence, I came at it from architectures and self-supervised learning, and the overlap turned out to be large.

So the pattern, if there is one, is that I was never trying to meet famous people. I was trying to get unstuck on a specific thing, and the person who happened to be stuck on the same thing was sometimes very good. The encounter was random. The collaboration wasn't.

r001.rationale: The response says each collaboration grew from a shared research problem and concludes that the collaborators were stuck on the same thing, directly explaining the encounters through alignment in their research concerns.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an element of chance in how you meet people, but whether that meeting becomes a collaboration depends on what happens afterward. You discover a shared interest, start exchanging ideas, and gradually build trust through working on a problem together.

Looking back, it’s tempting to connect those encounters into a clear trajectory. But at the time, you don’t know where they’ll lead. For me, the important thing is to stay curious and open—to engage with someone’s ideas without immediately asking what that connection will do for your career. An encounter can happen by chance; a collaboration takes sustained effort from both sides.

r001.rationale: The response mentions discovering a shared interest and working on a problem together, but does not explain the collaborations as arising from alignment in how the researchers understood research problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an element of luck, but an encounter and a collaboration are two different things. You can meet someone by chance; what happens afterward depends on whether you share an interest, whether you have something to contribute, and whether you follow through.

Looking back at my interactions with people like Kaiming and Fei-Fei, I wouldn’t describe them as steps in a carefully planned path. At the time, you’re curious about a problem, you have a conversation, and that leads to another conversation. Gradually, you discover that there’s something you want to work on together.

So I see chance as opening a door. Curiosity and the work you do afterward are what allow that relationship to develop. In hindsight, it can look very inevitable, but when you’re living through it, it’s much less clear.

r001.rationale: The candidate says collaborations develop through shared interests, curiosity, and finding work to do together, but does not clearly say they arise from alignment in the researchers’ understanding of research problems.
